summary: Psalm 24 begins by declaring that the earth and all who live in it belong to Yahweh because he founded the world. It then asks who may stand in Yahweh’s holy place and answers with a portrait of clean conduct, truthful speech, and those who seek God. The final lines call gates and everlasting doors to open for the King of glory, identified as Yahweh strong in battle and Yahweh of Armies.
whyItMatters: This psalm joins creation, worship, moral integrity, and divine kingship in one short poem. In Book I of Psalms, it gives a compact picture of approaching the holy God whose rule extends over the whole world.

context.author: The heading says, “A Psalm by David.” Psalms’ Davidic headings are ancient features of the collection, though readers debate whether such headings always mean authorship, association, dedication, or belonging.
context.audience: Israel’s worshiping and instructed community, and later Jewish and Christian communities that received the Psalms as prayer and Scripture.
context.date: The Psalms are an anthology formed over time; assigning one date to Psalm 24 from this chapter alone would go beyond the evidence.
context.setting: The chapter speaks of Yahweh’s hill, his holy place, gates, and doors, images that fit worship oriented toward God’s sanctuary without requiring a reconstructed ceremony.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetry and prayer, using questions and answers, repeated lines, and a climactic call-and-response about the King of glory.

outline.heading: Yahweh owns the world
outline.note: The psalm grounds Yahweh’s claim over the earth in his founding of the world on the seas and floods.

outline.heading: The question of access
outline.note: The poem asks who may ascend and stand in the holy place, then answers with clean hands, a pure heart, rejection of falsehood, and honest oaths.

outline.heading: The seeking generation
outline.note: The one described receives blessing and righteousness, and the group is named as those who seek God’s face.

outline.heading: The King of glory enters
outline.note: Gates and everlasting doors are summoned twice to lift up, and the repeated question identifies the King of glory as Yahweh.

keyVerses.text: A Psalm by David. The earth is Yahweh’s, with its fullness; the world, and those who dwell in it.
keyVerses.why: This opening gives the psalm its widest horizon: not only a sanctuary or one people, but the whole earth and everyone in it belong to Yahweh.

keyVerses.text: Who may ascend to Yahweh’s hill? Who may stand in his holy place?
keyVerses.why: The central question shifts from Yahweh’s ownership of the world to the human question of approaching his holy place.

keyVerses.text: He who has clean hands and a pure heart; who has not lifted up his soul to falsehood, and has not sworn deceitfully.
keyVerses.why: This verse gives the psalm’s answer about the kind of person who may stand before Yahweh: outward actions, inward orientation, and truthful speech are all named.

keyVerses.text: Who is this King of glory? Yahweh of Armies is the King of glory! Selah.
keyVerses.why: The final verse names the King of glory and closes the poem with a performance marker preserved in the text.

themes: Clean hands and a pure heart

questions.question: Why does the psalm begin with the whole earth if it soon talks about Yahweh’s hill?
questions.answer: The opening makes Yahweh’s claim universal before the poem narrows to the question of worship and access. The one approached at the holy place is not a local power only; the earth, the world, and those who dwell in it are his.

questions.question: What does “founded it on the seas” mean here?
questions.answer: The verse says Yahweh founded the earth on the seas and established it on the floods. Within this psalm, the point is that the world’s stability depends on Yahweh’s creative act. The poem does not pause to explain a physical model of the earth; it uses the image to support Yahweh’s ownership and rule.

questions.question: What is “Yahweh’s hill” and “his holy place”?
questions.answer: The phrases describe the place where Yahweh is approached in worship. The chapter itself does not name Jerusalem or the temple, so it is best to say only that the language is sanctuary-oriented. The question is not about climbing any hill, but about who may stand before the holy God.

questions.question: Does “clean hands” mean ritual purity or moral innocence?
questions.answer: In this verse the phrase is paired with “a pure heart,” refusing falsehood, and not swearing deceitfully. That means the psalm is speaking about conduct, inner orientation, and truthfulness. It should not be reduced to physical cleanliness, and it should not be treated as a full rulebook for every ritual question.

questions.question: Is the psalm saying only morally perfect people can approach God?
questions.answer: The psalm describes the person fit to ascend and stand in Yahweh’s holy place as one with clean hands, a pure heart, and truthful speech. Readers differ on whether to hear this mainly as an entrance requirement for worship, a wisdom portrait of integrity, or an ideal that exposes human need. The chapter itself emphasizes integrity without explaining every case of failure or restoration.

questions.question: Who is “Jacob” in verse 6?
questions.answer: The verse says, “This is the generation of those who seek Him, who seek your face—even Jacob.” In the chapter, Jacob names the seeking community in relation to God. The line does not explain whether Jacob is being used as a person’s name, a name for Israel, or a poetic shorthand, so readers should avoid pressing more certainty than the verse gives.

questions.question: What is happening with the gates and everlasting doors?
questions.answer: The poem turns to a summons addressed to gates and doors: they are told to lift up so the King of glory may come in. This language sounds like a formal, public welcome, but the chapter does not provide enough information to reconstruct an exact ceremony. The repeated lines make the entrance of Yahweh the climax of the psalm.

questions.question: Who is the “King of glory”?
questions.answer: The psalm asks the question twice and answers it twice. Verse 8 says the King of glory is “Yahweh strong and mighty, Yahweh mighty in battle,” and verse 10 says, “Yahweh of Armies is the King of glory.” Later readers, including Christian readers, have connected these lines with wider hopes, but the chapter itself identifies the King as Yahweh.

questions.question: What does “Selah” mean?
questions.answer: “Selah” appears in verses 6 and 10. It is an uncertain musical or performance marker, so it is safest to treat it as a preserved feature of how the psalm was transmitted rather than as a word whose exact instruction is known. It appears after the seeking generation and after the final identification of the King of glory.

glossary.def: The divine name used throughout this chapter for the God who owns the earth, gives blessing, and is named as the King of glory.
The place in verse 3 where the question of standing before Yahweh is focused; the psalm connects access to it with clean hands, a pure heart, and truthful speech.
A phrase in verse 4 describing the person who may ascend to Yahweh’s hill; in context it belongs with purity of heart and freedom from deceit.
The title used in verses 7-10 for the one who comes in when the gates and everlasting doors are lifted up; the psalm identifies him as Yahweh.
A preserved performance marker appearing in verses 6 and 10; its exact instruction is uncertain.
